subtopic: MERCHANT MARINE-GRANTS OR ALLOWANCES FOR WAR SERVICE
MERCHANT MARINE-GRANTS OR ALLOWANCES FOR WAR SERVICE
speechtext:
1.	Are any gratuities, allowances or grants paid to members of the merchant marine who served during the war years?
2.	If so, how do they compare with payments to those who served in the armed forces?
3.	If not, what steps have been taken by the government to grant these men gratuities and allowances?

subtopic: MERCHANT MARINE-GRANTS OR ALLOWANCES FOR WAR SERVICE
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Transport is concerned:-
1.	The monthly remuneration of able seamen was increased to a basic rate of $89.93, to which was added a war risk bonus of $44.50, making a total of $134.43 per month.
Income tax was paid on the basic rate only, war risk bonus and subsistence being exempted.
A special bonus of 10 per cent was paid on gross earnings, for a minimum period of six months' service in dangerous waters prior to April 1, 1944, provided a seaman signed an agreement to serve for two years or the duration of the war, or alternatively, signed an agreement to join a reserve of seamen to serve if called upon. Merchant seamen who have received a special bonus for service prior to April 1, 1944 are eligible to participate in the Veterans Insurance Act.
A war service bonus of 10 per cent on gross earnings was paid for service subsequent to
April 1, 1944 until the end of the war, for seamen who served on agreement or were listed as permanent employees of a Canadian company.
Leave on pay at the end of each year on agreement, at the cumulative rate of two days for each month of service, was allowed, together with round trip rail transportation
from a manning pool to the seaman's home, at the low cost of one-third of the one way fare.
Merchant seamen on agreement on completion of service were entitled to receive railway transportation from the port of discharge to their place of permanent domicile.
During service on a manning pool two year agreement a merchant seaman, if incapacitated for sickness or injury, received basic pay for a maximum period of twelve weeks.
Merchant seamen who qualified for the special bonus are entitled to vocational training to assist them to advance in their profession at sea.
Merchant seamen who left civil employment to serve at sea during the war are entitled to the benefits of the reinstatement in Civil Employment Act.
Pension for disability incurred from enemy action or counter-action is payable to merchant seamen serving on any Canadian ship, and to Canadian merchant seamen serving on ships of allied nations employed in service essential to the prosecution of the war. A disability pensioner is entitled to free medical care, with allowances during hospitalization for his pension disability, and is eligible to participate in the benefits of the Veterans Land Act and the Veterans Insurance Act. If debarred by their disability from following their former profession of seamen, they may be given vocational training under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act for any occupation.
In case of death from similar causes, widows and dependent children are pensionable.
A Canadian merchant seaman in receipt of a pension from an allied nation is entitled, during residence in Canada, to have his pension raised to the Canadian scale.
Merchant seamen detained by the enemy received a detention allowance, equivalent to their basic pay and war risk bonus, and also the special bonus. Dependents of merchant seamen who were detained by the enemy received appropriate portions of this detention allowance for their maintenance, the balance being paid to the seaman on his return to Canada.
Unemployment insurance coverage for merchant seamen came into effect on October 1, 1946, and by a special provision under the act

seafarers have been placed on a parity for unemployment insurance purposes with Canada's wartime armed forces. Under this provision many seamen are given credit for wartime service without payment of contributions after they have become established in insurable employment.
Medical and dental care is extended to pensioners while men on service are covered by the sick mariners fund and Merchant Seamen's Compensation Act.
2.	It would be very difficult to make such a comparison, inasmuch as the benefits differ so widely.
3.	Answered by No. 1.

Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Before this motion is debated, Mr. Speaker. I have a word of praise for Mr. Jules Castonguay, chief electoral officer. He is a most remarkable civil servant because he answers the letters he gets the day he receives them. He should be mentioned as an example to many others.
I have been interested in Mr. Castonguay from the beginning, when he was paid $4,000 a year. He was working very hard and was doing the work that another man, who was the grandson of a prime minister, did not do and for which he was paid $12,000. At that time I brought the matter up and was delighted that some consideration was given to Mr. Castonguay. He deserves special mention because he gathered the votes from all over the country at the last election. He has shown his efficiency. If he makes a recommendation to improve the act, I shall probably find it a good recommendation.
We have had experience of the unequal operation of the elections act. Before 1930 the election act was satisfactory; it was a good act. Between 1930 and 1935 it was changed by the administration of the day and made complicated and unsatisfactory. After the general election of 1935 the Liberal party decided to improve it. Then a committee met, in the daytime and at night, for a whole session, but it was impossible for them to reach a conclusion. The following session they met again. They fought hard, had bitter discussions, worked day and night, and finally made a report which was excellent, Do you know what it was, sir? The report recommended that the Bennett act be repealed and replaced by the previous act, something which could have been done by a very short bill without imposing so much work on the committee. But it was necessary to keep the members busy and to chase all evil thoughts from their minds. That is probably the only purpose achieved by the elections committee during the two sessions in which they worked so hard without accomplishing veiy much. My hope is that this time the members of the committee will not be fooled by such proposals, that they will have something serious before them and that their work will not be in vain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday evening last we were debating the omnibus bill, and I had a few remarks to make about controls. Today I should like to follow up the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on Friday when he proved to this house, as I believe you will agree, that controls are the essence of socialism. I say socialism cannot thrive without controls, and that socialism is contrary to human nature. That is my belief; and I address the house on this subject because on Thursday, March 20, the leader of the C.C.F. socialist party (Mr. Coldwell) laid down a challenge to this house to divide on this issue.

Emergency Powers
That is why today I choose to debate the subject that socialism is contrary to human nature.
First let me give a quotation or two. The first one is found in Benham's Quotations, and is from Dean Inge's book "Prognostications on Social Life in the Next Hundred Years". He says:
The three strongest instincts in human nature are religion, the family, and private property.
Where does socialism come in there? Then in another place he goes on to say:
What is called socialism is simply political bribery on a large scale.
There is only one period in history when socialism will work. That will 'be after the second coming, when we are in the millennium, but fortunately we will not need it then because we will have a 'better government. Lest you think I am biased in my quotations, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from something said by Pope Leo XIII on December 28, 1878:
Socialists, communists and nihilists strive to uproot the foundations of civilized society.
- That is taken from the New Dictionary of Quotations; and at another point in the same speech he said:
These monstrous views-these venomous teachings . . .
Just to show that the Roman Catholic church has not changed its views I quote from something said by Pope Pius XI on May 15, 1931:
No one can be, at the same time, a sincere Catholic and a true socialist.
My quotations today are not taken only from the clergy. I also have some from laymen, and here is what they have to say. In 1884 Herbert Spencer said:
All socialism involves slavery.
F. J. C. Henshaw, in "A Survey of Socialism", published in 1928, said socialism is-
The combination of religious sentimentality, industrial insanity and moral obliquity.
Then I quote the views of Mr. H. L. Mencken in "Prejudices" at page 109:
Socialism is simply the degenerate capitalism of bankrupt capitalists . . .
That is taken from the Home Book of Quotations; and in the same quotation Mr. Mencken goes on to say:
Its one genuine object is to get more money for its professors.
I return to the authority from whom I quoted first, Dean Inge, to quote a little couplet he wrote on the subject:
What is a socialist? One who has yearnings
To share equal profits from unequal earnings
Be he idler or bungler or both he is willing
To fork out his sixpence and pocket your shilling.
I have covered the clergy and the laity, Protestant and Catholic, but. I cannot for a moment forget one of our finest modern writers, one whom I am sure other hon. members admire as I do. I refer to Mr. Somerset Maugham, who once wrote a paragraph on this subject which I believe to be as pertinent as anything I have ever read. He said:
For all the vaunted hopes and promises- there is no single instance where socialism has succeeded in bettering the lot of the common man.
You may ask, Mr. Speaker, why I have put these quotations on record. I can answer that question in a moment by saying I have done this because I have a mandate from my constituency to oppose socialism in every form in which it may find its way into this house. In my constituency are men of all religions, all races and all creeds. Since it is in the heart of Toronto you may think it is dominated by Anglo-Saxons, but that is not altogether true. It contains a great many who have their roots in central Europe, many of Polish and Ukrainian origin, many from the Baltic states, and numerous others. These men, these European-born Canadians, know what socialist and totalitarian governments mean. They do not have to be instructed in what their relatives still in Europe have suffered under those governments.

speechtext: That is why their relatives in Europe vote for those governments every time they have a chance.

Alaclnnis) that these men whose roots are in Europe know what socialism means. They know what it is to have the iron heel of authority on their necks. They know socialism is an expanding doctrine, that socialist and totalitarian states are anxious to expand and to dominate not only Europe but this continent as well.

speechtext: We find socialism creeping in upon the country in a most interesting way. It starts with benevolence. Here are the great benefactors of the people, clothed with kindness, and with the purpose of raising up the common man! Then we move from benevolence to tolerance. As the next step they tolerate the views of the people. Then after tolerance we reach the point where they impose controls on the people. After controls there is enforcement; and after enforcement there is protection of those who are doing the enforcing. After that there is policing; and after policing there is the process of individual investigation. After that come the purges; and after that dictatorships-and finally tyranny and darkness. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Here is a quotation from the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, a socialist state. The New Dictionary of Quotations contains this:
The temporary victory of socialism in one country alone is possible, but its lasting victory in one country alone is impossible. That demands the victory of the revolution in other lands as well.
That is Joseph Stalin on Leninism, in 1926. I returned from the last war filled with admiration for the courage and bravery of the Russian soldiers who fought as our allies. But I cannot for one moment approve their philosophy of government, its teachings, its treatment of its own people or of some of the enslaved people in Europe. I am sincere in my belief that socialism will not work to the advantage of mankind. My socialist friends may be glad to hear that I am ready to admit capitalism is not all good. It has some abuses. But it is our privilege as members of a free parliament to rectify those abuses. Capitalism is subject to the law makers. We, who are the law makers, are subject to the electorate. The electorate are free to change their law makers at any time.
These times are not the times to be neutral; rather they are times to follow a positive course, to look ahead, to see the lessons of history, the lessons of the past.
In common with members of many other parliaments, we in this house have been accused by Major John W. Foote, V.C., of failing to lead the people. He is another Canadian who wears the Victoria Cross, in common with two members who belong to this party. At Fort William on March 23 Major Foote is reported by the Globe and Mail to have said that politicians are-
[Mr. Knowles.!
-mealy-mouthed and have not the brains in many instances to bring out a constructive programme.
He goes on to say:
"Too much narrowness and bitterness is sweeping the country today, creating a gulf between races and creeds. But problems of Canadians are simple in their elementary nature. Only interest and goodwill are required for a solu-tion."^ He had a word of praise for labour organizations that have purged their ranks of outside leaders.
Mr. CRUICKSHANK; He was speaking of Toronto.

speechtext:
No, I think he was referring to the part of the country my hon. friend comes from, as well. I have never noticed the hon. member speaking without prejudice. Then, to quote further from the newspaper report:
The country was in the most precarious stage of its history because of differences of opinion in various sections; there was more disunity than ever before.
I said that this is no time to be neutral, that the government would do well to follow a positive course, to trust the representatives of the people and listen to their advice. In the three sessions I have sat in parliament I have never heard either of those two hon. members, who carry the same decoration from His Majesty as is worn by Major Foote, advocate any policy in which they did not believe, or did not know was for the good of the country as a whole.
I plead with the government to forsake their controller mistresses in the ivory towers of Ottawa, and to return to the House of Commons the power to govern. This is the challenge of the times. What actually happened was that we went to sleep one night in the summer of 1945 and awoke to find atomic energy a reality-to find ourselves in a new world. History is on our doorsteps. Today we see the United States of America, a young and vigorous but perhaps immature country, summoned-challenged-to lead the world. We in the Americas must respond with her, to keep the flickering light of freedom alive for western civilization. If we in Canada wish to preserve our birthright of British freedom we must be intelligent enough to understand its worth, and we must fight with all our vigour against the inroads socialism has made on this continent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not have taken part in the debate had it not been for

Emergency Powers
representations made to me by a considerable group of electors who signed numerous petitions calling for the abolition of all controls. I shall deal later on with the matter of these petitions, and the information which I received from those whose names appear on them. What are these so much abused controls, after all? Judging from the tone of some members of the opposition one would be led to think that they are some sort of contagious, shameful disease. This may sound impressive to the unthinking, but to those who care to give the matter serious consideration, those controls are simply part of the law of this land, It is true that in these days this law of the land is much more considerable than it was a hundred years ago, or perhaps even fifty years ago. There is no question that the volume of federal and provincial laws and orders in council and regulations made thereunder has increased considerably. All this makes an imposing amount of legislation, but it is all based upon the proper legislative authority and hence it is the law of the land. Obviously all this legislation must have been good and desirable at some time and for that reason it cannot be condemned outright without a hearing. The most that can be said of some of these regulations is that they may have outlived their usefulness and should now be repealed.
The fact that very few of them have been singled out for particular criticism goes to show that the matter of their usefulness is generally recognized. For instance, the timber controls were debated with some amount of heat in this house on March 10 and we find that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) gave very good reasons for their retention. As far as I can recall, whenever any specific control has been attacked on the floor of this house there has always been a good reply made to the criticism.
A prominent British statesman, I think it was Edmund Burke, once made a remark in a jesting mood that the best governed country was the one with the fewer laws and the fewer taxes. That may sound all right to the unthinking, but how does it measure up to the facts? Listening to hon. members opposite one would think that they agree with such a statement, but I respectfully suggest that they compare our standard of living with that of other people who have fewer laws and fewer controls. Possibly there are a number of countries or peoples in Asia or Africa which are not burdened much with either laws or taxes. I am quite sure that the natives of Africa and of many parts of Asia are not in any way bothered by irksome 83166-106
controls such as the stipulation that they must cover certain parts of their bodies, but if one of those people were to look into our laws, usages and customs I am sure he would find that they are unnecessary and stupid restrictions which curtail unduly our freedom, and very likely he would denounce them with the same scathing language as that used by some hon. gentlemen in the course of this debate or the debate on the address.
Our modern civilization has become quite complex within the past century. In 1846 our population was mostly rural, and our farmers bought and sold very little. Industry was in its infancy and there were few manufactured articles compared to what there are today. Consequently trade was negligible in the terms of present day language. As we progressed our economy became more diversified, even to the point where our farmers are drifting into specialized farming, something altogether unheard of one hundred years ago. With an economy becoming daily more diversified, we need more laws and regulations if we are to benefit from our progressive specialization.
At this point I wish it to be well understood that I am not suggesting that our increased volume of laws and regulations is the cause of our material advancement. I simply want to observe that it accompanies it almost invariably in every country which enjoys a standard of living similar to ours as a result of greater industrialization and a greater diversification of production. There was a time in this country when we did not have any highway laws, and very little in the nature of game laws, liquor laws, income tax laws, and so on. Does anyone suggest that the degree of freedom enjoyed by our forefathers was more desirable than our present restricted freedom and increased social scurity? I think it is impossible to make progress along the line of social security unless we impose upon ourselves certain restrictions which do not inconvenience us to any great degree. Personally, I cannot say that I have suffered very much as a result of controls and rationing. On the other hand, like all of us, I have been inconvenienced by them on more than one occasion. And at this point I feel that I should take to task the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette) who is reported on page 1641 of Hansard of March 21 as having said:
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I have been surprised at the many weird fears of dire calamities which have been aroused by some hon. members in this chamber with regard to the legislation now proposed. Some have tried to make us afraid that parliament was prepared to give up its power to some external body; and they have gone on from that to talk about bureaucracy, regimentation and all the evils which they have been able to gather during the past few years from regimes which have been a disgrace to modern history. May I say that these fears, in my opinion, have been greatly overstated. Personally I have no fear at all about these things, and I hate them just as much as do hon. gentlemen who have opposed them. I do not for one moment believe, for example, that the right hon. gentleman who has led this parliament for more years than any other man in the history of Canada will deliberately give away the powers of parliament to somebody outside. I do not even believe that the Right Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would abuse the powers which we the other day permitted him to exercise in regard to a very important measure. I would not even be afraid of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) having similar powers conferred upon him by this house, which has the right and power to withdraw them if they are abused; for the people of Canada have the right and power to punish those who may be guilty of such abuse by discharging them.
In the past we have had to wrest our political freedom from great powers: kings, nobles,
lords and potentates; and still we have not possession of all the powers which the people must have. We must carry the struggle for democratic power into the field of economics. It is an extraordinary thing how hon. members can argue that a piece of legislation such as that proposed in the resolution before the house, which is to extend for a period of time certain powers which this parliament has never yet exercised except in time of war, could be represented as the abrogation of powers. It is the most extraordinary twist of illogical construction that I have ever listened to. I say, Mr. Speaker, we must not be simply content with the measure of political power the people have been able to obtain by their own efforts, despite the Conservative party in years gone by; we must gain economic power, and we must learn to use that power when we have achieved it. We must achieve it by democratic means, and we must learn to use it democratically. This means we must set up an entirely new technique, one which perhaps no one knows exactly how to proceed to organize, but one we must find as time goes by in order to exercise democratic power in the economic as well as the political field.
It took the crisis of war to reveal the need for the controls now under discussion, but peace has its crises as well as war. The resolution before us is to provide for the extension of those powers, taken in time of war, for a limited period, and I desire to join with the leader of this party in protesting against the willingness of the government to release these powers too readily at the urging of the private interests who are most concerned and the political parties who would like to serve them. The government, in following a policy of decontrol, appear to me as happy as children going to a circus when they can announce that they have let go something to which they should have held on. They have already given up many of the powers they should have held on to. This legislation is a proposal to continue some of those powers for a time, but the object eventually is to release all controls and go back to the old method of allowing the economic powers of the country who are personally interested to determine the economic course of this nation.
I want to impress upon this house that the economic pursuits of this nation are going to be controlled by somebody. They always have been controlled by somebody, and that control will be continued. It is of vital interest to the people of this land whether those controls are exercised by the people themselves in their own interests, or whether they are to be exercised by those interested only
Emergency Powers

in their own personal gain. The questions we should be asking in regard to controls, and which really should not be applied to this measure at all, are these. Who are going to control the economic destiny of Canada in the future? How are these controls to be exercised, and what is to be their purpose? As I see it, sir, there are just two alternatives before us. The one is to allow those who own and control the great basic industries of this country to determine, in the interests of their own profits, what shall be the economic policy of Canada henceforth. That is one course. The other is to find a way of democratically controlling our economic destiny, through the democratically elected representatives of the people.
I have been astounded, too, at the way those who profess to believe in democracy can express such dire fears of power, as we have heard some hon. gentlemen in this house. Some have even boasted that they have no plans and do not desire power. In this respect I would refer particularly to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). Both these hon. gentlemen have exhibited great nervousness over the possibility of having too much power, for fear they might be corrupted. But I have seen no nervousness on their part in respect to the powers now being exercised by certain individuals and corporations over industries which affect the lives of all the people of this country. I should like to ask the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario what he will do if by some chance, some day, he might become chancellor of the exchequer or minister of finance. Then he would have to prepare a budget. That is a great power, because a budget will affect the lives of all persons in this nation, from the baby in the cradle to the man in the :offin. Everyone will be affected, so it is a tremendous power. What will the leader of the Social Credit party do if he becomes prime minister? According to his own philosophy, announced in this house from time to time, he will be on the horns of this dilemma. Either he will have to permit himself to be corrupted by the power which goes with the office, or he will have to divest himself of power to the point that he will be completely useless. That will be his choice. A government without power and without a plan is the most perfectly useless institution in the world. Canada can very well do without a government that has neither a plan nor the power to carry it into effect, because such a government is nothing but a blundering, expensive, useless dummy. Government is government only to the extent that it has power. A government
[Mr. lrvine.l
is a good government only to the extent that it uses its power wisely. A government must have a giant's power; but I agree with the great Shakespeare that it had better not use that power as a giant sometimes does. There must be no competing power within the nation that can equal the power of a government; otherwise you have no government, because government is where the power is, whether that be in the factory, in the bank or on the treasury benches; and in most instances in Canada that power is still in the factories and the banks of this country. The real power of democracy is amongst the people themselves, and, as I say, they must have more power than any other body within the nation. A government without power is like a steamer without steam, like a car without gasoline, and I have my suspicions of people who are afraid to use power when they are asking for it.
Why do these people who are so anxious to get power express such fears of it? All power is dangerous in the hands of incompetents. The power of steam is a destructive power. It can blow up the boiler, wreck the establishment and kill everybody within a certain range. Atomic energy is a great power, and a dangerous and destructive power, but it may also be a very constructive one. Power may destroy, but power can also fulfil. Without power, however, we can do nothing in any government. I repeat that the important questions are: Who has the power; how is it to be used; what is it to be used for?
The danger in a democracy is not in having power; it is not in its using of power. The danger in a democracy is the abrogation of its powers, and the allowing of irresponsible people to use powers which ought to be in the hands of the representatives of the people.
It is assumed, theoretically at least, that the power of the people is supreme in a democracy. If the representatives are not to use that power, then who is to use it? I assume that the only practical way in which the people of Canada can use their power is through their representatives in parliament. It may be that we shall find some better mechanism as time goes on; but for the present that is the only way we have been able to devise. The old village moot is gone, and we have found it necessary to send representatives here to carry on the work of the people. They, from time to time, give power to ministers of the crown who are responsible to parliament, powers which are essential in order to carry out certain essential public services.
That is how our democracy operates; and until we find a better way for democracy to express itself we must adhere to those

methods. Those who fear power should neither seek it nor be entrusted with it. Some hon. gentlemen are fond of quoting in the house the alleged aphorism of Lord Acton. I say it is an "alleged" aphorism, because it is not true. The so-called aphorism is this, that power corrupts-that absolute power corrupts absolutely. I have heard that from this corner of the house until I am tired of hearing it.
It is more clever than it is wise, Mr. Speaker. The most absolute power in human affairs in a democracy is the power of the people themselves. No autocracy or dictatorship in history, whether it was a so-called absolute monarchy or an absolute dictatorship, has thus far been able to withstand the absolute power of the people. The czars, the kings, the Hitlers, the Mussolinis, the potentates-they have all been humpty-dumpties on the walls of power, and have been thrown down by the absolute power of the people. They are not anything today but the dust of a disturbing memory.
Therefore I say to you, sir, if the leader of the Social Credit party believes that absolute power corrupts absolutely, then the democracies of the world are the most absolutely corrupt of all bodies whatsoever, because they have the most absolute power. Indeed, by the application of that assinine aphorism they are condemned to inevitable corruption. That is the logic of the Lord Acton parrots.
The fear of power implies the negation of all government. There can be no government without power. The fear of power indicates a lack of confidence in oneself to do the job of representing the people. The fear of power implies a lack of confidence in one's fellows, and lack of faith in the democracy of which he is a part. This distrust in ourself leads to our passing the precious, if dangerous power, to others, so that it can be used by them even against us, instead of our using it on our own behalf.

But when a government taxes much less from them than the monopolists did, and leaves them with much more, what do they say? They say, "We won't milk cows for Ilsley." That is what they say. "We don't mind milking cows for mortgage companies; we don't mind milking cows for monopolists; but when it comes to milking cows to pay taxes to our own country, which money comes back to us in social services-no, we won't do that."
That is exactly the same attitude of mind as that of those who are afraid to exercise the power which democracy has conferred upon itself, and which we as representatives of the people are charged to uphold and exercise in the interests of the common people.
We are not taught in a similar way to fear the power of the profiteers, the power of the monopolists. It is suggested we ought to fear our own power, but never to fear the power of the profiteers or monopolists.
It is strange with what complacency we permit the most potently coercive power, namely that enjoyed by economic Hitlers, to dominate our lives, while we are so afraid of using power ourselves. I do not understand men who fight against delegating a portion of power in our possession to a minister, or to a board for which a minister is responsible, but who would not fight against the power now exercised by a corporation to use or not to use, or to misuse, the means by which all must live.
It is time we distinguished between power exercised by dictators and that exercised by a prime minister in a democracy. In the latter case the power is in our own hands, the hands of the people. We can delegate it or exercise it or withdraw it, at will. It is power that has never corrupted any government. It has been the power which governments refused to use-the economic power-which has corrupted governments. It is because we have never taken over economic power that it has been used by those who have it to corrupt public life, because they could not get what they wanted in any other way. Some public men in our history have succumbed to it.
Some writer has expressed the idea-I forget who it was; at any rate the idea is capable of standing on its own feet-that "He who fears what he must face exhibits symptoms of mental sickness; and until he is able to face what he fears he is not on the way to mental health."
I suggest that we must face this question of power; we cannot get anywhere without that

behalf. The danger is always greater when power is in the hands of people other than in our own. This government or any other government in a democracy is simply a machine driven by the power of the people. To say that we must not use our own democratic power to control things which otherwise would destroy us is nothing short of political insanity.

The British government was drawn into this argument by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). I must say that I agree with that hon. gentleman when he says that we should never follow blindly what any other government does. While I agree with him on that, I would say also that we should never fail to follow a good example, no matter what government sets that example. I notice that the hon. gentleman is the subject of an editorial in today's Ottawa Journal. He is now regarded as the one Liberal left; not a left Liberal, but the one Liberal left. I believe the hon. member for Quebec South is a very good Liberal. I agree with many of the things that he says and does. I like him, but I do not like the company he is now in. I am afraid of his Liberalism when he gets the support of the Journal. I do not know whether the Journal knows he said in his speech that, while he disagreed with the idea of copying any government, if he had been in Britain he would have voted for Labour. If the Journal knows that, perhaps it will take -back its support and the hon. member for Quebec South will be all right yet.
I think the British government have done some good things about which we ought to know. First, they have revealed that planning and controlling can be done without dictatorship. Second, they have shown that nationalization preserves all the advantages of large-scale production achieved by monopoly without any of the disadvantages of monopoly. Those are significant things for us to know. In this connection I should like to quote what I regard as a brilliant passage from a speech recently made in the British House of Commons by the Prime Minister of Britain. He said:
The British people will show that in peace as in war democracy can be combined with strength, tradition with progress, liberty with self-discipline and prosperity with social justice.
I want now to reply to some of the things that have been said by one or two hon. members who have preceded me in this debate. I am replying to them because they seem to think it is socialism that is covered by the resolution and not the extension of the meagre

power which has been practised by this country for years during the war. I shall refer first to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming)
[DOT] who charges the government and the C.C.F. with taking power from parliament to transfer it to somebody else. If that were the case I am sure the hon. member would be the first one to vote for it. However the very opposite is the case. We are not transferring power; we are taking a little more power than we ever had before. What is the point of his argument? What we want to do is to continue the power proposed in the resolution; it as a matter of fact we want to extend. He wants to discontinue the exercise of these powers. That is what this debate is about. He is the one who is trying to give powers away or to allow the powers that this parliament has never exercised to remain in the hands of those who have always exercised them, apparently according to the pleasure of the hon. member for Eglinton.
The hon. member says that the Progressive Conservative came here to fight for the supremacy of parliament. They are 600 years late. The supremacy of parliament was fought for by the British people right in the very teeth of Conservative opposition throughout all history. For an hon. member who has as fine a mind as the hon. gentleman; for an hon. member who has the education he has been privileged to have to rise in his place and make an absurd claim of that kind with respect to parliament is nothing short of extraordinary. It has been the traditional position of Conservatives to retard democracy, to prevent the people from having their votes, in every way possible to hold power from the people. That is their tradition.
I do not charge deliberate totalitarianism to the Conservative party. I do not like to charge that to any party, because most of those who talk that way have just got hold of a stinking term that they like to apply to the policies of other parties in order to frighten the people. But while it is not perhaps totalitarian in its intentions, it is certainly totalitarian in its policy. If I wanted totalitarianism in Canada I would vote for the Conservative party. They want total economic power vested in private interests- private monopoly.

The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is never afraid to say exactly what he thinks, and just three or four minutes after the hon. gentleman who is one of his colleagues sat down he blurted out the truth without the slightest hesitation. He said that business large and small has been clamouring for freedom from so many controls. My hon. friend should realize that he cannot have it both ways. If he does not get off that fence he will tear his breeches for certain.
I wish to say something now with respect to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). He reminded me somewhat of a helicopter. He flew over the whole empire of economic problems, but hovered here and there over very interesting spots, and then, when you thought he was going to make a landing, he roared away and never made a landing at all. I agree with him, however, on one thing. He said:
There can be no democracy at all without economic freedom.
I thought he was going to land on that spot, but if he had he might have discovered something about what economic freedom means. Economic freedom and monopoly cannot go together.

There is no such thing as state monopoly except in the minds of those who do not understand the meaning of terms, and I shall deal with that in a moment because the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) dealt with it. He said:
There is actually no difference between a state monopoly and a private monopoly.
Just because a man says that with great unction does not make it true. Private monopoly is a one-man show, and he gets the proceeds of the gate; a public monopoly is everybody's show and they all get the proceeds of the gate. Private monopoly is a privilege held by an individual or corporation at the expense of all the rest of the community. A public monopoly, if you wish to call it so, is where the common people, all the citizens, are shareholders and have equal benefit in the so-called monopoly. If that is not a difference there is no meaning in the English language.
Then the hon. member went on to say:
The only effective controls are those which are inherent in a justly scientific structure.
Now, sir, that is the largest mouthful of sweet nothings I have ever seen anyone take at any one time. Not knowing what it means, I have to pass it. I will not say that the hon. member had nothing in mind, but I will say that if he had anything in his mind when he said that it is still there. He was anxious that we should define our terms. I ask him to define the terms in that statement. He then went on to advocate the establishment of a monetary authority charged by parliament with the responsibility of maintaining a constant balance between effective purchasing power and available goods and services.

The hon. member said that the best way to plan is by competition of consumers with dollars as ballots and they will vote with their buying. Well, that is nothing like a plan; that is not planning anything. For the hon. member's information let me quote something of what that kind of thing does. This is a quotation from the brief presented on February 2, 1937, to the royal commission on textiles by Elie Beauregard, K.C., commission counsel. He said:
It is destructive competition that maintains wages at a low level. When responsibility does not rest with foreign competition, it lies with domestic competition waged at the expense of the worker and resulting from the wage inequality between provinces, cities, towns and villages.
Let me give another brief quotation from an official document of the British government which will give some idea of what happens when you leave things to the dollar votes of the consumer and have no regulatory plan for a national industry. This is in regard to electricity and reads as follows:
At present Britain suffers from the inconveniences of total absence of standardization in voltages or appliances. In 1936 there were as many as forty-three different declared voltages for low and medium pressure supplies, ranging from 100 to 480 volts. A citizen moving from one part of the country to another, or from one London district to another must often scrap the whole of his electrical equipment because of these divergencies.
That is the sort of thing which calls for planning. It is not enough to let anybody buy just what he likes so that when there are shortages the first thing that would happen is that all our sugar would go to the making of candies and they would be bought at high prices by the sweet-toothed people who have money in their pockets and the rest of the people would not have anything. But I must not take the time to develop that, because I believe I have just about exhausted my time and I should like to finish what I have to say.
I intended to take up the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette); I think he needs someone to take him up after what "Little

Chicago" did to him a little while ago. I shall conclude, sir, by saying that planning means balancing all the needs of the nation against all the available resources of the nation; balancing the man-power demands against the available man-power; balancing the needs of factories, housing, transport and other public services against each other; balancing the need for exports against the need to keep at home products which are essential to the lives of the people within a given country. These are some of the things that are meant by planning. Therefore, sir, I am getting tired of the evangelism of private enterprise, of the ranting about bureaucrats, regimentation and the death-knells of freedom when we suggest that parliament must be supreme in economics as well as in political policy. I would say that hon. gentlemen who carry on a programme of that kind are mental monstrosities limping frantically across the political stage on crutches.of hate.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote for this resolution and for the bill on the continuation of controls, not because I find it pleasant, but because I deem it necessary to do so. Furthermore, I support this legislation because of its urgency and its temporary nature. Were it neither urgent nor temporary, I would oppose it, because to my mind it would be unconstitutional. I may add that on that score, the majority of my colleagues from the province of Quebec are of the same opinion. I submit this with all the due respect for the decisions of the Privy Council and I take this opportunity of thanking the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) for the explanation which he has just given us. His statement of Thursday last had left a few aspects of this legislation out of focus, but now that the measure is recognized as constitutional, everything seems to be quite clear. I thank him once again and I congratulate him for having shed some light on the matter.
It is in order, I believe, to compliment the government on allowing Parliament this year to legislate on controls. I must admit that last year I felt some misgivings about supporting bill No. 15, which maintained the government's right to rule by orders in council.
I believe that the sooner we revert to the true allotment of legislative, executive and judicial powers, which constitute the very essence of our parliamentary democracy, the better it will be for the true interests of the Canadian people.
It is the duty of Parliament to enact laws and appropriate the money required for the management of the country's affairs.
It is the function of the government to administer those laws and to manage the money voted by Parliament.
Finally, the courts are required to give an interpretation of the laws and of the Constitution when disputes arise between citizens or between citizens and the Government. However, it is not within the jurisdiction of the courts, whichever they may be, to change the laws or to modify the Constitution.
Those are elementary principles of constitutional law, but it is advisable to bring, them, to the attention of this house from time to time, for, unfortunately, they are too frequently disregarded nowadays.
In a debate on controls and planned economy such as this one, if hon. members indulge first in electoral propaganda and then give their attention to the legislation under discussion, if the house is turned into a public forum instead of legislating, there are a large number of useless speeches and unending discussions. I suggest that parliament does not accomplish its true function which is to study and legislate.
If, on the other hand, instead of putting it up to parliament, as was done in the case of this bill, the government enacts too many orders in council, it transgresses the prerogatives of parliament. This should happen only in extreme cases, under quite exceptional circumstances, such as war.
And while it is the Government's duty to govern and to manage, if it allows its planned economy to be managed by boards and bureaucrats with no responsibility to the house and to the people of Canada, the cabinet surrenders part of its rights and privileges. Such practice, if allowed to last, will eventually distort the spirit of the constitution.
Then again, if a court, such as the Privy Council for instance, instead of merely interpreting the constitution of this country, takes upon itself to change it on the grounds that the central authority may encroach upon provincial rights, even when there is no urgent necessity to do so, this court is not exercising purely judicial functions. Instead of merely interpreting the law, it changes it, and in so doing trespasses upon the legislative powers of this country's parliament.
It then becomes a cause not for amusement but for genuine alarm to see the keenest champions of provincial autonomy acting likewise as the most ardent advocates of appeals to the Privy Council. Such inconsistency is nothing short of appalling.
In closing, may I express the hope that this measure for the maintenance of controls will be discontinued as soon as practicable in the best interests of the whole country.
Finally I hope that the necessary distinctions between the legislative, executive and judicial fields will henceforth be more and more closely observed, so that our constitution will operate as designed by the fathers of confederation.

My chief point of appeal is to ask the government to reconsider, even at this hour, the resolution now before the house. I ask it to bring in bills so that parliament may decide that which may best be continued or discontinued. I realize, of course, that this procedure would take more time. But after all, with our future at stake, with the welfare of Canada, the welfare of the Canadian people and the whole economy of our country at stake, surely it would be best in the long run to do what I have suggested. We have already granted an extension of time of these emergency powers until May 15. It would be possible no doubt if these bills were not concluded by that time to seek a further extension, but in the meantime parliament, the elected representatives of the people, the voice of the people would be heard so that they might place their stamp of approval or disapproval on the bills as they were presented to this house.
I think we all feel greatly concerned at the trend today in world events. Canada is in position to give a certain type and degree of leadership in world affairs. We have reason to expect that leadership. We have

Now they talk of our supremacy at a time when we can go on to greater things with the initiative and background and enterprise of our people. Are we to turn back the pages of history and seek to begin the struggle all over again? Balancing the needs of the nation, says the hon. member for Cariboo, but I ask him who in his group sitting in this house today would he feel capable of balancing the affairs of a great nation? Where would he find the ability or the initiative or the understanding of the complex problems of industry and finance and development that he would seek to have placed in the hands of someone who would tell you or me what we should do?
I think the time has come when we must seek to break the shackles and bonds that are binding us, so that we may have an opportunity for greater expression, greater advancement and greater development. Then Canada will indeed find her way to the leadership which she is capable of providing. In this great land we should seek to encourage those who believe in freedom, those who believe in democracy to come to our shores. We shall not get the people we would like to have as long as we have on our statute books legislation which provides for the continuance of the very things many of them are seeking to escape from in distant Europe.
I can see the trend today in Great Britain. We have a great stake in the British isles. I am not going to condemn the British government, but I am going to say that, unless they change, Great Britain is indeed in for a difficult time. We find that today they are seeking to import hundreds of thousands of workers to do the work which Britishers formerly were able to do for their nation. It is theoretically possible for one to agree that something should be done to hold down the cost of living and yet to be afraid that the something that has to be done interferes with liberty and freedom and therefore might be at too great a cost. As a matter of fact, this whole position was presented to the .house most forcibly this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine). It does seem to me that we can too easily become the victims of certain cliches, and one of these cliches is the supposition that the protection of freedom involves only protecting the individual against the state. That has been the ultimate position stated in this house by those who claim to represent the essence of liberalism, and I agree that the day is not gone when we must watch in a democratic way to make sure that the state does not make inroads on the life of the individual.
But, Mr. Speaker, the thing that I should like liberals-with a small "1"

to bear in mind is that our main concern is to protect the individual against anything that interferes with his freedom and his liberty. In the days of our grandparents, if they were protected against the authority of the state, well and good; but in our day that is not sufficient for the protection of the individual. A person's life depends upon the cost of living; it depends upon whether or not there is full employment; it depends upon whether or not there is a market for the produce of the farmers and whether that produce can be disposed of in an orderly fashion. There is a whole gamut of things that bear on the life of the individual today which our grandfathers knew nothing at all about, and in that situation governments have a new responsibility; they still have the responsibility not to be bureaucratic or interfere with the liberties of the individual, but in addition, they now have the responsibility to protect the individual against the things over which he has no control in the economic order.
Our lives today are not cast in the simple environment that our grandfathers had; they are cast in a complex world where, underlying our very existence, underlying life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, is the whole question

Emergency Powers
of how the economic system functions. I maintain that those who claim to be liberals, those who claim to be concerned about protecting the freedom of the individual, must be concerned about the freedom of that individual against the caprice and the depredations of the economic system. And so it seems to me that all this talk about bureaucracy, about state monopoly being just as bad as any other, is a case of well-meaning individuals failing to think the matter through.
The liberal position-and I am still using the small "1"-is a great position, but it is a position that needs to be thought through and worked out in terms of the kind of society we have today, and in that society what is needed is responsible democratic government that protects the individual at every point where he needs protection.
It has been said a good many times during the course of this debate that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) has introduced a socialistic measure into this house. He has been chided by my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party and my hon. friends of the Social Credit group for this action. The attempt has been made to pin the word "socialist" on this bill in the thought that that would condemn it. Let it be said quite clearly, Mr. Speaker, that this measure is not socialism. This measure is a device to save capitalism. My hon. friends to the right are missing the boat completely when they rise in opposition to it. This is a measure that would save capitalism in Canada from the kind of chaos that the Minister of Justice rightly described the other night; and if that happened, there is no telling where this countiy might go. We of this group are not anxious to protect or save capitalism, but we do believe in orderly progress. We want to move on in an orderly fashion from what we now have to democratic socialism, and I pause for a moment to thank those who have taken the trouble to call attention to the fact that we in this group are socialists. We want to move on in that direction.

As I say, our contention is that the main fault of the government in connection with this whole measure is not that they are asking for powers beyond those which a democratic government ought to have in order to protect the interests of the Canadian people, but that they do not exercise the full responsibility which those powers involve.

Mr. Speaker, I have been one of the more or less appreciative audience listening to the numerous speeches, pro and con, for and against the resolution now before the house. There is an old saying that too much of anything is not good for one. We have had a great many speeches; I have listened to most of them, and now I should like to take about five minutes to vary the monotony as far as I am concerned and offer a few words on this important legislation.
I believe this matter of controls resolves itself into something not only of domestic but also international concern. I believe it places before this parliament and the people of Canada a problem that is of extreme importance in view of the disorganization that exists today in a world weary after many years of war. Right now this. country is faced with the challenge of solving these problems which face us in this period of rehabilitation, and we must bear in mind that in this conflict-if we may call it that-we are confronted with threatening forces just as terrifying as those which obtained in time of war. This should be the leading issue in the minds of our people today.
Fortunately we in Canada are in a better condition than most people in the world, including even our allied friends, because Canada is today economically sound. After the depleting war through which we have passed, I believe much of the credit can be attributed to the ex-Minister of Finance and the gentleman who until recently was chairman of the wartime prices and trade board. These men stood at the lines of defence when the country was in great danger, and not only combatted but hurled back what I might describe as the fifth columnists, those selfish interests which fain would break through the lines and put our economy into a state of chaos, even at a time when the government was enduring the stresses and strains of war.
The superior position enjoyed by Canada today, after a depleting war, certainly cannot be attributed to accident. As I said earlier, I believe our present economic soundness can be traced to the controls which obtained during the war. Is it not reasonable that in this conflict we should go cautiously and carefully before we eliminate or withdraw those measures which have done so much for Canada in time of war?
Let us not forget that, while Canada is enjoying the fruits of a victorious war, we are today engaged in a conflict that is just as important and just as serious, and bids fair to be just as enduring as the conflict of war. In those circumstances I believe it is just as essential that we should preserve the same precautions which operated so beneficially during the time of the greater stress of war.
There are those who advocate that all controls should be removed entirely and immediately. I believe people who hold that view disregard the best interests of millions of our people. It may suit some of the selfish interests, but certainly it is not to the advantage of the masses of the people of Canada.
Fortunately we have in Canada today a government that is very little concerned with the selfish interests of the few. We have a government which takes great concern in the interests of the masses. I have every confidence that the government will not continue one control which it considers unnecessary. I have the further faith that from time to time the government will be willing to make changes in any of the controls it considers should be maintained, so as to eliminate any factors in those controls which would tend to penalize any particular individual interest.
During the war there was a certain element that undertook to belittle and to hamper our remarkable war effort. I am afraid that today there is under the surface an element that is undertaking to hamper the progress of the efforts made by this government in the present conflict which, as I said before, is just as serious as was the conflict of war.
In war we had the dread of defeat. Right now we are threatened with the dread of economic collapse. This is too serious a time to be thinking about politics, or to think about the few who would gladly take this opportunity for their own aggrandizement, and to promote their own interests. I say that today in this conflict the government are given the same mandate they were given in the time of war. They did their part well by 'bringing us out of that struggle in a sound economic position. They have a mandate in the present conflict, a mandate of administration. That mandate is to meet present problems and to give leadership. Today I say they are giving that leadership. The government has a difficult and dangerous task to undertake, and I say that we must use the same generosity and have the same degree of tolerance, even to the extent of making some sacrifices, if we are to win this important conflict in a time of peace. Our very sons who went out and shed their blood in order that we may have prosperity
Emergency Powers

in Canada, and so that we may have peace, have sown the seeds of peace on many soils. It is the responsibility of the government and of the Canadian people to cultivate that soil so enriched by their blood, and to see that that harvest of peace and prosperity for which they fought will be worth reaping.
I hear a great deal about bureaucracy. One would almost think the government's action is such as might be expected from Hitler. But as a Canadian, and one who will live in Canada so long as his span of life continues. I would be more happy living under an authoritative rule administered by responsible ministers of the crown, men who have done so much in the handling of controls, than I would be if all those controls were removed and those selfish interests were given the green light to proceed to the practice of that policy which they fain would undertake, for their personal aggrandizement and in disregard of the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, many people are asking the house to do away with controls. Some of those people think this move will favour their political publicity, some others have the intention of protecting their personal interests, and others take that stand because they think that if controls were lifted the flow of commodities would be resumed through the natural channels of trade.
In order properly to inform the fair-minded people, having in mind the welfare of the population of Canada, I have made a careful study of the subject and I shall now proceed to outline the conclusions at which I have arrived. If the government were to lift controls immediately I think everyone will admit that a large number of tenants would be thrown out of their homes. Since there exists at the present time an acute shortage of houses in this country, it does not require much imagination to foresee the perturbation which would result throughout Canada. Farmers and proprietors of houses do not realize what would be the distressing situation of tenants dislodged from their farms or homes, who would be at a loss to find shelter within the means of their pocketbooks. It is evident that the price of rent throughout the occupies rented quarters, and these people country would be increased tremendously. As a general rule it is the labouring class that occupies neeed an immediate increase in their wages to face this sudden additional increase in their budgets. It is evident that under such circumstances the cost of manufactured articles would have to be increased in proporfMr. McGarry.]

I sincerely believe that if we have the patience to wait a little longer before releasing more controls it will be possible to do so without creating too much disturbance of our economy. Every fair-minded member in this house will certainly realize that the government is not asking for the continuance of these controls for its own satisfaction. So far as I am concerned-and I know there are many others who share my view-I hate this interference of the government in private business.
In one of my previous speeches in this house I drew the attention of hon. members to the fact that I suffer personally from these controls. I have to sell the production of rayon yarn made in one of my plants at the same prices as prevailed on October 11, 1941, namely, seventy-five cents to 81.40 a pound when I could dispose of my production on the New York market at prices varying from $1.40 to $2.60 a pound f.o.b. shipping point. We produce in another plant ladies' shoes which retail in Montreal at from $6 to $9, when the same shoes are being sold at from $20 to $25 in Washington. I use these two items as an example only because I am familiar with them. I think they prove that it is against my own interest to favour controls. On the other hand, what lasting benefit could I expect from a situation in the United States which is bound to collapse at any moment? In the fact of such a precarious and dangerous situation, I prefer to carry on business on the basis of 1941 and not expose my country to an indescribably chaotic economic situation in which I would be engulfed with the rest of the Canadian population.
The government expects to reduce its expenditures next year by $900 million. This is interesting news for the population of Canada, but what is more important is the stabilization of prices without which we would be in the same situation as now exists in the United States where the purchasing power of 1947 salaries is lower than that prevailing during the war, even though there have been substantial increases. Salaries in the United States have increased eighty per cent. Weekly wages in industry averaged $25.20 in 1940 for thirty-eight hours. At the beginning of 1945 these had increased to $47.50 for a week of forty-five hours. The increases in wages have been completely wiped out by the lifting of controls in June last, except on rent, sugar and rice. In comparing the increases which took place in the prices of commodities and wages, the United States secretary of labour
admits that the purchasing power of salaried people is seventeen per cent inferior today to what it was during the war.
Since the decrease in the expenses of running the government of Canada, as announced in the federal budget, must reflect a decrease in taxation, the normal consequence should be a decrease in prices. Instead of a decrease in the prices of the necessities of life, it seems that we are on the threshold of a new wave of increases. Some controls have been abolished on some products and prices have increased. Any overvaluation of prices would absorb at least part if not all of the benefit derived from a decrease in taxation. The salaried man would not be any better off. At a time when employment is reaching normal and products and goods of all kinds are reappearing on the market, this man would notice with consternation his diminishing buying power. By that very fact his situation would become helpless. Scarcity of goods caused by the war does not free him from purchasing the necessities of life. He would then be compelled to ask increased wages or strike.
It is easy to prove to him, with indisputable figures, that he is the loser when he goes on strike. On the other hand, increase in salary, which will serve as a pretext for an increase in prices of goods, will create inflation and by the same fact will destroy the benefit foreseen by the increased wages.
Under ordinary circumstances the increase of prices should create abundance and should thereby correct the evil through the law of supply and demand. But unfortunately this scheme cannot produce any satisfactory results to prevent inflation owing to the fact that consumers need too many things at the same time.
During the war the government has assumed control of the economy in this country. Through many mistakes, it has nevertheless brought about useful and indispensable corrections. While our war effort has created an abnormal situation, requiring controls, we have to face the same situation today which is created by an unlimited demand for all kinds of products.
It is not the proper time to relax controls which are still in existence, and it is to be hoped that the government will receive the authority to maintain this policy for a limited period. The members of this house have so fully realized the importance of this precarious situation that when a vote was taken on the transitory measure presented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) on March 18, 177 members voted in favour of the measure while only thirteen members voted against it.

In some requests which I received asking for the suppression of controls I notice there was also a demand to prohibit exportation. Needless to point out, we have an unfavourable balance of around $500 million with the United States for the year 1946. This means we need foreign currency to finance our importations. Moreover, if exports were prohibited how could we dispose of our wheat, bacon, cheese and other manufactured articles that we must sell to other countries if we want to maintain and preserve the position that this country has acquired in the world. If one takes into account the overvaluation of prices in other parts of the world compared with Canadian prices, he would certainly admit that suppression of controls would create an increase in the exports of our products and thus increase the scarcity of same on the Canadian market.
For the above-mentioned reasons and for many others which would take too long to enumerate, I believe that maintenance of existing controls for a certain period is not only useful but absolutely necessary if we want to maintain a sound economy in our country. I understand that proprietors deserve sympathy because they are the most affected, but in face of two evils it is natural to choose the lesser. I would rather see the proprietor rent his house on a cheap basis than witness the renters being thrown out om the street. It is to be hoped that the competent authorities will give preferred attention in the near future to the urgent ease of the proprietors.
If I listened to some of my electors who have not given much consideration to the matter I would vote against the controls. In so doing, I am sure I would please them. Unfortunately the duty of a sworn member of parliament does not consist only in pleasing electors and himself but rather to take the interest of the Canadian people at large, no matter how disagreeable his attitude might be on such an important matter.
Before taking my seat, may I draw the attention of the minister to some decisions of the officers of the wartime prices and trade board, which are unjust and detrimental to the interest of Canadian citizens. Personally, I have been the victim of one of their decisions which was far from being equitable, though the case, after different stages, had to be decided finally by Mr. Gordon himself.
Recently a firm in my constituency made application to the timber controller to extend an export permit from 1946 to 1947 because their timber could not be shipped last year, on account of the lack of cars. The permit was refused by the timber controller on the ground that it was not the policy of the board

to consider such requests. I do not know the salary being paid to this officer. I imagine he must earn many thousands of dollars yearly. What is the use of paying such a high salary to this officer if he refuses to use practical sense in face of uncontrollable circumstances? A clerk with a weekly salary of $25 could do the job. As a matter of fact, it does not require much experience to tell the people that the rules and regulations of the board must be observed. Though many additional cases could be told the house, I will not mention any more. However I will suggest to the minister that he appoint a committee composed of a few members of the house to reconsider unfair decisions of the wartime prices and trade board officers. There must be someone to judge and straighten out the actions of these officers when their decision is detrimental to the welfare of our citizens. I think this suggestion is a protection which we owe to our people when they cannot obtain justice from our bureaucrats.
I have been told by many of my colleagues that my suggestion would not be accepted by the minister because the officers of his department would not approve it. I have too much confidence in the honesty of the minister to believe this. I am convinced that if my suggestion is not acceptable to the minister, he will find some means of establishing some kind of control over the officers of the wartime prices and trade board. If he does not, I leave it to him to bear the responsibility of his inaction.
When I take the responsibility of voting for a measure of this kind wffiich is very unpopular in many parts of our country the least I can offer to my electors is that I have taken every precaution so that they may enjoy some kind of assurance that their cases will be fairly dealt with.	.

Mr. Speaker, when he introduced this resolution, the Right Hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) expressed the wish that we wait until the second reading of the bill to fully discuss this measure.
His suggestion might be just and reasonable if this were an ordinary piece of legislation; but when I know that at this very moment a large part of the people on the north shore are undergoing hardships that may be even worse than those endured by the populations of conquered countries; and when I know, as I shall show in a moment, that those hardships are the direct result of the imposition of "controls", you will readily admit, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot pass by a single occa-

Emergency Powers
sion of protesting against that policy of controls which the government want to maintain.
I say right now that I am far from joining in the praises of Mr. Gordon which we heard last week from certain corners of the house. Our national economy was much too long under the "control" of that man, a real dictator, who did not even have the decency to answer telegrams such as those I sent him and in which I nearly pleaded with him to grant the people of my county permission to obtain the necessities of life before winter had set in, when it is too late to have them brought over to the north shore.
The country in which we live is regarded as essentially democratic, but the claims made by the official representative of 70,000 Canadians carry no weight in the eyes of such bureaucrats who have no responsibility to the people.
