subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Had I been speaking in the name of a few financiers instead of pleading the cause of 70,000 Canadians, there is no doubt at all but that I would have gained a better hearing.
The present legislation is placed before us with consummate skill. We admit readily that it may be necessary to control certain economic activities such as the relations between landlord and tenant. But on the plea of necessity, the government are asking us to pass various measures, every one more unconstitutional than the other.
Even as regards rentals, I deem such legislation to be unconstitutional. As I said in this house in 1945, the dominion government should allow provincial legislatures to adopt similar measures, if they are considered necessary. Let us once for all return to the provinces the rights guaranteed to them by the federative pact.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in support of my opposition to this measure, I shall not indulge in academic discussions. In the last twenty-five years, when I had to plead cases before the courts of my country, I always made it a point to present facts, and once the facts were proven, draw conclusions. I should like to present a series of facts which, I am convinced, will substantiate my opposition to the continuation of controls.
I might explain, in the first place, that my constituency extends over a distance of 900 miles on the north shore of the St. Lawrence; in the Charlevoix section the population is composed of farmers, whereas the Saguenay district is inhabited by fishermen. The last 600 miles of the St. Lawrence north shore are also inhabited mostly by fishermen, and no
lands suitable for cultivation is to be found there. Therefore the fishermen depend on supplies shipped to them from Quebec city and Montreal. As the hon. members know, navigation in that large section of the province of Quebec is usually interrupted at the end of November. It is absolutely necessary, of course, that those people bring in adequate food supplies for the winter season, which extends from early December to the end of April and even into May, before it is too late. To those people, as to anyone else, milk is one of the prime necessities of life. Unable as they are to obtain so much as a drop of fresh cow milk on the coast, they naturally have to bring in evaporated milk all the way up the north coast. As a provident people, who know they must not wait till the very last days of fall to bring in needed provisions, by last Augu^ they had come down to Quebec and Montreal in an attempt to secure goods to carry them over the winter. I have just called them provident. Knowing they sometimes have to put up with much hardship, they generally provide as best they can for possible emergencies. For all the makeshift means at their disposal, they none the less insist on taking the best possible care of their health. And here, Mr. Speaker, may I quote parts of a letter I received early last January from Dr. Currie, a member of the International Grenfell Association and the hospital "superintendent at Harrington:
(Text):
I am a newcomer to the coast and only here for the winter months, having practised in the city of Regina, Saskatchewan, for twenty-one years, then bought a fruit farm near Toronto, Ontario, and one year ago retired but came out of retirement to give a hand out down here.
I have been here only two months but have covered all settlements from Romaine to Blanc Sablon and am starting on the second round trip tomorrow, weather permitting.
Thought you might be interested in the medical aspect of your constituency. As you perhaps know, health conditions are not what they should be.
Deficiency diseases are rampant, such as bad teeth in both old and young, poor vision, susceptibility to skin diseases, all due to faulty diet, lack of fresh fruit and vegetables and the essential minerals. Estimate over 1,000 people with scabies (itch) and impetigo along this coast. This is generally being brought under control. It is not due to dirt or unclean bodies in these people as I have been amazed at the cleanliness of their bodies, have not even seen a pair of dirty feet.
Many cases of gastritis, duodenal ulcer and gall bladder disturbances, due usually to indiscretions of diet. These respond to proper diet usually.
Have seen a number of cases of high blood pressure, mostly in women over 50 years. This I did not expect to see at sea level.

(Translation):
So, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the living conditions 'of the inhabitants of the north shore are normally very hard, but when they are worsened by the implementation of control measures such as those that are in force we are bound to arrive at the results described by Dr. Currie in the report he sent me.
I said, a while ago, that last year, these people tried as usual to get their supplies in as early as August last. Here is a letter from one of the most important merchants of Natashquan, Mr. Emilien Landry, an excerpt of which I shall read to you. The letter is dated August 26, 1946:
During my last trip to Quebec city, early in August, I wish to make arrangements to order my stock of evaporated milk for the winter and, at the time I was there, on August 3 to be exact, an order was issued forbidding all or nearly all shipments of evaporated milk to the north shore, for the reason, I was told, that more milk had already been shipped to that district than in 1941.
See how intelligently the controls are. administered. In August 1946, a good looking man, comfortably seated in an office in Ottawa or in Toronto, learns that the people of the north shore have had more evaporated milk than in 1941, it matters little whether they lack food during the coming winter. He decrees arbitrarily that no more milk will be shipped to those people.
Which meant that milk was the object of a black market on the north shore. At least, that is the answer I received on the occasion of my visit to the office of the board in Quebec. On the other hand, I cannot see what outlets we could have had for such a black market, considering navigation facilities we now have at our disposal, namely, two boats that call at the same time and do not show up before another fortnight.
How ridiculous it is for the representatives of the prices board to make such an assumption when we know that all the places I have mentioned on the north shore are isolated from each other! How can it be said that those people were in the black market business? With whom could they have traded?
Moreover, they cannot leave their place except to go fishing a few miles off shore. Their only means of communication with the outside districts is the boat which calls every two weeks.
However, as soon as I found out about the situation to which the people of the north shore were being subjected, I at once tried to get in touch first with the office of the prices board at Quebec. Unfortunately, I did not obtain satisfaction. In passing, may I say that all the officers in the Quebec branch of the prices board gave me, in this and 
every other instance, their full cooperation; however, they were unable to do anything. They had to follow the instructions of the controllers. At the end of August, I described our plight to the Quebec office of the prices board to the best of my ability. I then received from an official of that board a letter dated September 6, from which I quote the following excerpt:
As stated in the course of our telephone conversation, Saguenay county is a "free zone" as far as the rationing of evaporated milk is concerned. Wholesalers operating in "restricted zones" and requiring extra coupons to cover their deliveries to free zones should apply directly to the wholesale administrator, Metropolitan building, Toronto.
In other words, Quebec and Montreal merchants wishing to supply the population of the north shore with condensed milk had to request permission from a Toronto gentleman who had not the faintest idea of conditions prevailing in our province.
Towards the end of August and the beginning of September, I received a great many letters from merchants all along the north shore complaining about the restrictions to which they were subjected. Some of these are really pathetic. In September, realizing that they would be caught by the oncoming winter season without supplies for the children of their district, therefore, still trying to help these people-it was my duty to do so-I contacted the controllers in Ottawa and Toronto but unfortunately, I obtained no satisfactory results.
Incidentally, may I quote a wire which I received on September 6 from the mayor of Sept-Iles who explained the said lot of his fellow citizens:
Please contact Mr. Hugh Cree, distributive administration, Toronto. Village in sad plight without lard or condensed milk. No farmers in district. According to physician's report, submitted today, many children suffering now. Please understand we plan for six months ahead, being cut off during winter season. Heard today from our wholesaler that 1,600 cases of milk for north shore are frozen by government. Would appreciate prompt reply.
J. R. Vigneault, Mayor of Sept-Iles.
About the same time I received another letter from Godbout in Saguenay county. Let me read from it the following excerpt:
Ordinarily, I buy from 50 to 60 cases of evaporated milk for my store during the winter season. But now I have no way of securing it. If existing conditions continue, we shall be unable to obtain milk for the winter and our people will go without milk for their children.
The dealers have milk that could be sent to the coast, but they are under government orders not to do so.

Emergency Powers
During the same period, I received a similar letter from the mayor of Riviere-au-Tonnerre. On September 5, when I had come to the conclusion that it was impossible to correct this abnormal situation through the wartime prices and trade board's officials in Quebec, I sent a message to Mr. Hugh Cree, wholesale retail food director, Metropolitan building, Toronto, explaining the predicament of my constituents. My message was dated September 5. On September 9, four days later, as I had no answer from this controller, I decided to send another communication and finally, not having yet received an answer on September 10, I thought that as a member of parliament, representing a population of 70,000, I might at least get in touch with Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the prices board. I therefore sent him on that day a message of which I have here a copy, giving him a clear and lengthy description of the near plight of my electors and asking him, as a special favour, to remedy that condition. On September 13, having received no answer from Mr. Gordon, I presumed that my message might have been overlooked and I sent another, urging him to kindly take whatever action might be needed to help a population and specially children who, without his assistance, would in all probability have to endure very severe hardships. But Mr. Gordon did not take the trouble to answer. Little did he care for the Canadians along the north shore.
A few days later, on September 12 or 13, I received from Mr. Hugh Cree, of Toronto, a letter from which I quote the following excerpt:
(Text):
In an effort to correct the situation and stop the distribution of needed reserves, suppliers in restricted areas were reminded that shipments into free areas such as the north shore must not exceed basic quotas.
(Translation):
Note this, Mr. Speaker. The controller himself told me that the north shore people drank more milk than usual this year and will therefore have to do without for the rest of the winter. The children of the district, scattered along the coast, will have no milk next winter; such is the decision of the controller.
While we are deprived of this essential commodity, our government is doing its utmost to push it on the export market. According to information supplied in answer to a question which I asked recently, Canada produced, from August 1945 to July 1946, 198,394,000 pounds of evaporated milk. During the same period, we shipped abroad 62,423,900 pounds of this product while Canadians on the shore line did without. The controller had decided to deprive them of milk because this year they drank more than in 1941.
Such are the fruits of the control policy. Some people may claim that these are a few isolated cases; but I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this bulky correspondence in my hand, these exchanges of telegrams, these numerous telephone conversations are proof enough that our dictators were not in the least concerned about the plight of the north shore people. Furthermore, I maintain that many cases similar to the ones I have just mentioned could be brought to our attention by other members. I am convinced that the same situation exists in various constituencies of my province and elsewhere. We had reached November, and still our people were clamouring for help.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to quote a few excerpts from a letter which reached me on November 18, 1946, almost on the eve of the closing of navigation. It was sent to me from Riviere-Moisie:
I have just written to you about an application I have filed for a permit to secure Carnation milk. I had asked permission to obtain 60 cases for the winter season. It is two months since I have had any to sell. I had been counting right along on that permit, but now I have been advised that I will receive only 10 cases...
We have no milk for sale here; the other dealers have none either.
As the season is far advanced, it would be necessary to ship the milk next week, for the longer the shipment is delayed the greater the risks of freezing. I am counting on you as I know that you are aware of our plight, especially that of our infants. Mothers are wondering how they will feed their babies, as there are a large number of them and all are fed on Carnation milk. It is not logical that we should allow our own children to starve in order to send our foodstuffs overseas.
Those are the letters which I have received from the merchants of the north shore during the months of August, September, October and November, 1946. But I was unable to obtain from those gentlemen of Ottawa and Toronto the permission to send supplies to our merchants. Finally, in December, I succeeded in obtaining a small portion of their requirements. May I, on behalf of my constituents, thank sincerely the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) for the help which he gave us when, at the end of December, it was necessary to enlist the services of an ice-breaker in order to send foodstuffs to the north shore. As the river had frozen over, navigation was closed in all the bays of the shore. Hence it was necessary to use an ice-breaker in order to send supplies to the merchants. As I said just now, these are facts, amply sufficient to show that the government's present policy in the
Emergency Powers

matter of controls is absolutely nefarious. Against the facts I have adduced, nothing has been advanced so far but theoretical considerations. It is claimed that frightful chaos would follow in the wake of decontrol, but I have yet to hear facts in support of such a claim.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this control policy. I feel that the people of this country should no longer be subjected to the whims of bureaucrats. I know that Canada has all the resources required to avoid a predicament such as I have just described. If it were proved that certain controls are still necessary, then, Mr. Speaker, the government should assume its responsibilities. Let the ministers assume responsibility, let them take away dictatorial powers from irresponsible bureaucrats and when I have cause to complain of conditions such as I have just described, I shall know just what minister to blame.
(Text):
Mr. PATRICK H. ASHBY (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, I was going to claim sabotage, because I have been squirming about in my seat, jumping up every little while during the past two hours, and I am sure I have worn my pants as much tonight as ordinarily would be the case in a month.
Canada is a big business, with a great many branches such as agriculture, mining, transportation and so forth. This great business is owned by its shareholders, the citizens of Canada. I do not know who would own this great business but the people of Canada; and when the matter of controls comes up I immediately ask myself: control whom, by whom, and for what purpose? The greatest of all controls is taxation, and I went into the library for the sole purpose of reading up a little on taxation. I opened the encyclopaedia and noticed one quotation from what I must assume to be the greatest authority in the world on this matter. I called the librarian and asked if he would obtain for me the book by that author. In about the time it would take me to pluck a chicken he brought it to me, and here it is. I see a page boy has just brought me some water. I hereby christen this book, representing orthodox political economy, under the name of "Bureaucratic BlancMange". I should explain what I mean by blanc-mange. That is a French word meaning nothing more or less than plain, ordinary cornstarch pudding, spelled "pudd'n". Perhaps I should explain what I mean by bureaucratic blanc-mange. It does not matter what problem may face us; it does not matter what
TMr. Dorion.]
definition we seek, there is only one place to go for the answer. That is back to nature, so let us go back to the farm.
My wife has reminded me that unless I go over my hives we are not going to get the honey we deserve. So of course I ask her where I left this, that and the other thing, as is natural with most husbands. She tells me where I left everything, and I gather up the various odds and ends required, such as a bee veil, a smoker, an old piece of sacking, some matches, some toothpicks to pry into suspicious looking cells, a little pair of scissors to clip the wings of the queen, and a hundred and one things including a notebook and pencil to keep a record of each hive, and I start off toward the hives looking like Robinson Crusoe. But I am stopped by my little daughter, who pulls at my overalls and says, "Daddy, if I help you with the bees will you give me all the honey from one hive"? What father could refuse such a., request? Taking note of her delicate little hands and fingers, I see an opportunity to have that child pick up the queen bee so that I can clip her wings without injuring her. I arrive before a hive, ready to operate, as it were, and I say to my daughter, "A little anaesthetic", meaning a little smoke; I tap on the top of the hive, indicating that 1 am coming in; I ask for the hive tool, and open up the bowels of the hive exposing the combs. I lift out a comb. There on the bottom are queen cells, and I begin to cut them away. My little girl notices a specialized substance in these cells and inquires what it is. So I explain that a queen bee lays eggs, that when those eggs hatch out they are fed a normal diet and worker bees emerge. Fed a specialized diet, drone bees emerge. They are the ones that live on the products of the toil of the others. Fed a highly specialized food called "royal jelly", the larvae will hatch out and turn into royal queens.
I take one of these cells, about the size of an elongated thimble, and squeeze a glob out of it and offer it to the child, saying, "Taste it." She, being like her mother, keeping one eye on business and the other eye on me, says, "You taste it first." Well, I can't very well back out, so I take some in my mouth but I immediately turn my face from her because it shrivels up my tonsils till they are like a dried prune; the roots of my back teeth shimmy in their sockets and I am rendered temporarily cross-eyed. However, with a gulp I quickly recover my normal composure, face her again and say, "There, you see; it is all right." She asks, "You didn't spit it out?" and I truthfully reply "Oh, no, I didn't spit it out. I swallowed it,

Emergency Powers
and now it is your turn." I squeeze a great glob of it, including the wriggly larvae, or maggot, into her pretty little mouth. The immediate result startled me, for she licked her pretty little lips, looked up into my face and said, "That's pretty good stuff, eh, daddy?" The ultimate result, however, was astounding; for ever since that day the child has stood at the top of her class in school, and I have become a member of parliament.
This bureaucratic blanc-mange is very similar to royal jelly, because if this is fed to unsuspecting, gaping, gullible students they are certain to turn into bureaucrats.
I now open the book, and here are two full pages of testimonials. Let me read just a couple of the shortest, just one sentence. Here they are from Leland Stanford university; Brimfield, Massachusetts; the Idaho Industrial Institute; Boston university; the university of Chicago; Liege, in Belgium; Columbia university, the university of Kansas, the university of Texas, Yale university and so on. Here is a short testimonial by one of these professors of political economy:
It contains admirable features, and I shall recommend it to our students.
Here is another:
It is, I think, the best . . . treatise that I have read. How clear and simple it is!
This, hon. members will understand, is the real cat's whiskers. Let us see what this man says in regard to taxation. He starts out by saying, "First of all, students, you must never forget"; that is the way these professors, with profound dignity of deportment, speak to these poor, gullible students. He says:
First of all, it is to be remembered that taxation . . . may be looked upon as a blessing...
That is his opinion. My opinion is that it is a blessed evil-and I believe my opinion is just as good as his. But listen to what he says further on:
Taxation stimulates individuals to endeavour by increased industry and economy to repair the breach taxation has made in their fortunes.
Can you imagine that! In other words, if you are out fishing in a rowboat, with your family, don't let the kids know, but just carry a small axe along with you, and knock a hole in the bottom of the boat. The whole family will be stimulated with renewed efforts to repair the breach you have made in the boat. And that is the sort of bureaucratic blanc-mange that is fed to students in this day and age.
Let us have a look at these bureaucrats. At the time of confederation they claimed, mind you, that we owed a tremendous amount of money. They said we owed $93 million. Under 33166-108
their careful, painstaking, thorough and efficient supervision it increased to S500 million in 1912, to $544 million in 1914, to $1,000 million -a billion dollars-in 1917, to $2 billion in 1919, to $3 billion in 1920. In 1939 it was $3,710 million and in 1946 it was $17 billion. And these bureaucrats want us to hand over controls to them today! Can you imagine it!
Here are the shareholders of this great business of Canada, which has been so wonderfully prosperous and has produced untold wealth in coal, in food stuffs, in oil and tar sands, in everything imaginable under the sun. And then these bureaucrats actually tell us we have been operating at a loss. Don't believe it. It is not true. I claim that the people of Canada, the shareholders of this business, have been robbed and deceived all these years into believing that these bureaucrats have been doing their duty faithfully, when in fact they have been sabotaging the resources of this country, which belong to the people. That is why we say it is time an accurate and true record was kept of our business and a dividend paid. I am certain of this, that no country in the world can show such prosperity as Canada. No business in the world can pay such dividends to its shareholders as can this dominion.
I am a farmer, a practical one, and it grieves me to know that the people of Canada, who are so trusting, will actually permit themselves to be so sabotaged. Look at this, as an example: In 1944, in hogs alone we produced 8,863,830. And we produced them at a time when the majority of our able-bodied young men and women were away from home. Taxation officials were not imposing such restrictions upon us at that time; they were leaving us alone. But no sooner was the war over than the enemy set its troops on the farmers throughout western Canada. They have not bothered the people in Quebec, because they know very well what would happen there. And that is right here in Canada. It is a domesday book; that is true.
It is an old trick, as old as the hills. Here is the communist manifesto. What does the second paragraph in the list say? It says that there must be a heavy and progressive or graduated income tax against all the people. Is that not what we are doing now? robbing them of their hard-earned money and rendering individuals dependent upon the state. That is the only objective of taxation -to enslave the people of this country.
What in the world are we doing today, I wonder? Why, at the time of the Petition of Right, the people were not afraid of kings. Listen to this. Paragraph 4 reads:
Resolved that the ancient and undoubted right of every free man is, that he hath a full and absolute property in his goods and estate, and that no tax, tallage, loan, benevolence or other like charge ought to be commanded or levied by the king or any of his ministers, without common assent by act of parliament.
The whole issue at stake at that time was *between members of parliament-the House of Commons-and the king. The whole fight today is between the House of Commons-hon. members who sit here-and the bureaucrats, and bureaucracy. Are we afraid of bureaucrats?
In the year 1100, in connection with the Arabs, I read this:
Eleven hundred years after the birth of Christ we find conditions very similar to our own existing. Taxation reached burdensome proportions, farms were neglected, soil robbed of its fertility, sand storms, dust storms, plagues and famine stalked the land. The people finally revolted against socialism and communism and once more began anew.
That was away back in the year 1100. It states further:
The subjugated people shared in a common fate of excessive taxation and oppressive rule. No wonder if under such conditions no creative work in art or literature was produced.
That was written by Professor Philip K. Hitti, of Princeton university, in his book, "The Arab".
Now let us see what has happened to our hog production. It is reported that in 1944 we produced 8,863,830 hogs. Last year the production had dropped to 4,465,159, or a loss of nearly 4,500,000 hogs. These bureaucrats would tell you that it is because Mars winked at Venus, and she let him down, or something of the kind. They will give you some excuse. If these bureaucrats do not know the results that are going to ensue they ought to be fired, discharged-dishonourably discharged-from their duties. That is what I would do, if I were in a position to do it. There would not be a deputy minister in his office tomorrow morning.
Can you imagine the shareholders of this great business, the people of Canada, being insulted and ruled by these dictatorial bureaucrats?

That is a serious charge. The people of Canada can and, I believe, should demand the arrest of every deputy minister employed in every department and place them on trial for the serious offence of high treason. I think we would get some Tesults if that happened and I should like to give evidence at such a trial. The power to tax is the power to destroy and that is the only reason why they have usurped this power.
Away back in the time of Charles I, the people through their representatives protested against government by order in council. The authority for the forced loan at that time came from the council. Those who refused to pay, those who revolted against that undemocratic compulsory law were examined by the council. The protest of the members of parliament was that the council was taking upon itself both the functions of the judicial courts and those of parliament, and that is exactly what these bureaucrats are doing today.
Let us see what the Lord Chief Justice of England has to say about this. I do not think any other country in the world can claim to have greater justices than those to be found within the British empire. I should like to quote from the book, "The New Despotism" by Right Hon. Lord Hewart of Bury, and I read from page 11 as follows:
A little inquiry will serve to show that there is now, and for some years past has been, a persistent influence at work which, whatever the motives or the intentions that support it may be thought to he, undoubtedly has the effect of placing a large and increasing field of departmental authority and activity beyond the reach of the ordinary law.
And later on:
... a despotic power which at one and the same time places government departments above the sovereignty of parliament and beyond the jurisdiction of the courts.
And again:
That there is in existence, and in certain quarters in the ascendant, a genuine belief that parliamentary institutions and the rule of law have been tried and found wanting, and that the time has come for the departmental despot, who shall be at once scientific and benevolent, but above all a law to himself, needs no demonstration.
And again:
It is that the whole scheme of self-government is being undermined, and that, too, in a way which no self-respecting people, if they were aware of the facts, would for a moment tolerate

. . . the goal ... is to subordinate parliament, to evade the courts, and to render the will, or the caprice, of the executive unfettered and supreme.

It was reprinted in 1945. I noticed a small .article in the Edmonton Bulletin by Harold L. Weir, a very wise man, which I should like to put on the record because it bears directly on this matter. It reads:
Decline of Parliament
There is no doubt that the power of the Canadian parliament and especially the power of the House of Commons has declined seriously in this generation. This gradual undermining of parliamentary authority may well be regarded as the most sinister development of this age.
The Canadian constitution, that is to say, the constitution of tradition as well as of statute, was developed on the democratic principle that primary governmental authority should be vested in the smallest units of government and the larger units should enjoy residual authority.
In other words, all government possible for the municipality to effect should be in the hands of municipal or civic councils. All affairs which are beyond the municipality but are within the scope ol the province, should be left with the provincial legislatures. Inter-provincial or foreign matters are clearly the business of the central government at Ottawa.
The present trend is decidedly away from this basic principle.
Thus, the current dispute between the provinces and Ottawa is clearly more than a question of subsidies and taxation. It involves centralization of control in Ottawa. And that centralization of control is daily violating to a more alarming degree the democratic structure of this country.
Every power that is stripped from the municipality or the province is an unhappy step towards the fascist system.
During war time, centralization of control was perhaps an emergent necessity. Some vestige of central control may be essential while the nation moves into normality again.
But it is utterly wrong to argue that centralization must be maintained on the grounds of efficiency because efficiency is not the first consideration in a governmental system.
Efficiency is an excellent objective. But when the steps taken to secure efficiency destroy even better objectives, efficiency can become dangerous.
Freedom of enterprise, for instance, is infinitely more vital than mere efficiency. And controls necessary in a war economy can very easily become intolerable bonds once the need for them is gone.
Italy wras translated into a corporate state to give the people employment and to "make the trains run on time." These w-ere splendid pur-83166-1081
poses. But in the achievement of them the Italian people lost their freedom and very nearly lost their souls.
I he centralization of power became so great in Italy that the common man became a slave.
And that is the great danger today in Canada. Once we restrict the right of the common member of the Canadian Commons to have a free voice in every public policy we will have lost much of our democratic right of governing our-seflves. No matter what is gained in efficiency or financial yields or even administrative economy, the loss in democratic freedom is frighteningly greater.
The Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley to the contrary, the cabinet must be the servant of parliament. It governs the country, not by a divine right, but by the will of the people. Once wre assume that governmental power is derived from elsewhere than the people's will, we are throwing overboard the very fundaments of democracy.
The member who permits himself to be dominated by a party whip is untrue to his functions. When a man is elected to represent a constituency, he must raise his voice in behalf of that constituency no matter what his party says or thinks.
Does that practice prevail today? It is so rare as to be practically non-existent.
If liberal and democratic ideals are not to go into eclipse before an encroaching fascism or a protesting socialism, the early power of parliament must be restored. The necessities of the war years must cease to shackle democracy.
It is only too easy, because Ottawa presently holds the purse strings to sometimes surrender rights for security.
It is an evil deal. To trade freedom for security is a precarious business. To have security without freedom is to be in chains.
I happened to discover quite by accident the cause of our difficulties. I played hooky the other night and went down to see some of the members of those adorable creatures the fair sex skating at the ice carnival. I paid $2 for my seat, but I lost about thirty-five cents worth of my enjoyment when my mind was bi ought back to parliament. Of course I went there because I could see more of these beauties than I ordinarily could on the street and therefore could admire them the more. I asked myself the question, how on earth can any human male possibly avoid marrying one of them? In fact I think so much of them that 1 would have married a half dozen of them by this time if my wife had not kept her eye on me and I had not watched myself pretty closely. How on earth any young Canadian could possibly sit on a sofa with one of these lovely creatures and edge away from her is more than I can say. Right then and there it struck me like a bolt from the blue that Canada has suffered for over a quarter of a century from bachelor administration.

Within the past few days these price reductions have been announced, running in' some instances to as high as a ten per cent reduction in the prices of certain types of tractors and machines. The disparity in the purchase price of automobiles, as most people know, in each country is at least twenty-five per cent greater than is the disparity on farm implements. More than that, the people employed in the United States receive a greater remuneration for their services than people working on like jobs do in Canada. That is also recognized, and the point there is that the standard of living is higher in the United States than it is in Canada.
Some mention was made this evening about the production of live stock in this country. The greatest production of hogs for market in the history of Canada was in 1944, and that rather on a sound economic basis as compared with some of the controls we have developed in the later years. Out of a total of 8,863,178 hogs, 5,768,046 were produced in the prairie provinces where the grain was also produced to feed the animals. Alberta led all provinces that year, producing 2,981,940 hogs. In 1916, Canada as a whole produced only 4,465,161 hogs. May I also add that during 1945 there were in Canada some 6,760,000 beef cattle, and of that total 3,596,000 were in the three prairie provinces.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that I interrupted the crossfire that was going on. I can assure you that I enjoyed it as much as other hon. members did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext:
If the hon. member waits until we are through, he will be more pleased than ever. I would also say that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) presented his case in an able manner; and while I cannot agree with him in his line or argument, at the same time I believe that both he and I have something very much in common, namely, that we both consider this to be a much too serious business for us to enter into the frivolous side, as we sometimes do. I can assure you, sir, that, like the hon. member for Souris, I shall not endeavour to emulate the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Ashby).
The question before us is one of great concern to all the citizens of this country. In my humble opinion, this house and the country are divided into three camps. One is a small but sometimes very vocal minority, speaking for a small minority in the country, which would do away with controls willy-nilly, so that those who would fatten on the necessities of the people would have their way. The other group, as I see it, is represented

in this house by a small number, also representing possibly the same proportion out in the country, who would like to do away with controls. In fact, they are anxious to decontrol as fast as possible, but having taken hold1 of the tail of that pussycat they do not like to let it go or possibly are alarmed at the consequences if they did let go. In the third camp that I mentioned are members of this group. While we are in a small number in this house, I believe that we are speaking for the large majority of the people out in the country, the citizens who are vitally affected by this question of control or decontrol. We believe that we are speaking for them when we say we need these controls just as much to win the peace as we needed them to win the war. It is my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, that, had the government not undertaken the controls which they did undertake during the time of war, our road to victory would have been much more difficult, if not even impossible.
My leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and other members of this group have since this debate began, placed on the record in an able manner the stand we take, and it is not my intention to belabour the point much more this evening. In fact, I can assure you, sir, that it had not been my intention to take part in this debate at all until a certain question was brought into it by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey). In my opinion, it was ill-advised on his part, and, if not irresponsible at least misleading, when he made a statement that no sincere Catholic could be a true socialist. He gave only part of the story. He took only one short sentence out of the paragraph. I know where he took it from. It is in the encyclical quadragesimo anno by the late Pope Pius XI, from which the hon. member for Trinity took that one small sentence:
No one can, at the same time, be a sincere Catholic and a true socialist.
I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat at the moment, because in the short time at my disposal this evening I hope we may have this question straightened out once and for all. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is with the utmost regret I find it necessary to enter into a discussion of this kind. Had the hon. member read at least the whole paragraph, the story would have been quite different. The heading is, "Catholic and socialist are contradictory terms". The late pope said this:
If, like all errors, socialism contains a certain element of truth (and this the Sovereign Pontiffs have never denied), it is nevertheless founded upon a doctrine of human society

Emergency Powers
peculiarly its own, which is opposed to true Christianity, "Religious socialism," "Christian socialism," are expressions implying a contradiction in terms.
I would point out that when this was written the Conservatives had not yet established a contradiction in terms by adding to their name the word "Progressive". Times are changing. I would say that the church to which I belong condemns in no uncertain terms the type of socialism that interferes with a person's religious beliefs, which is opposed to Christianity and totally opposed ;o the ownership of private property; and that .s the only kind of socialism the church recognizes as such. I would point out further for the benefit of the hon. member that as the years have gone by, we have had many different kinds of socialism throughout the world; and for want of a better term we have applied to the philosophy and principles of the C.C.F. the expression "socialist", because the fundamental principles of our policy are to build laws around the protection of society rather than the protection of capital. I would also point out to the hon. member if he were in his seat that I take my religious instruction from the authorities of the Roman Catholic church and do not need to go to Tory Toronto for it. Eight years ago, almost to the day, I had to rise in my place in the legislature of Saskatchewan and tell a Liberal of like mind that I did not need to take my religious instruction from the Liberal party. I never thought I would be called on to rise in my place in this august chamber and deal with a matter of this kind.
As I mentioned, there are different kinds of socialism. I am not attributing any motive to the hon. member for Trinity, but why did he bring this matter into this debate at this time? I know from experience that on different occasions people have tried to put me on what they called a spot by asking, "Are you a socialist? If so, you cannot be a member of the church to which you profess to belong." I say that politics in this country have reached a very low level if we must put up with that kind of thing. Those people should stop and consider how unfair they are. For instance, if I were to ask the genial and honourable Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) "Are you a Christian?" his answer certainly would be, "By all means." Would I then be justified in saying, "Oh, but you are a member of the Salvation Army"? Or if I were to ask the hon. member for Trinity, "Are you a Christian?" he would certainly and quite properly answer, "Yes, by all means." Would I then be justified in saying, "Oh, but you are 83166-109
one of Jehovah's Witnesses"? I ask for a little fairness in these things. Ever since I have been around in the world I have adhered to the teaching of my father, which was, "Let every man practise his religion according to the dictates of his conscience."
I said a while ago I wanted to get the record straight. I have another quotation from the same encyclical from which the hon. member for Trinity took one small sentence. Here is a paragraph entitled, "Domination has followed from free competition." It goes on:
In the first place, then, it is patent that in our days not alone is wealth accumulated, but immense power and despotic economic domination is concentrated in the hands of a few, and that those few are frequently not the owners, but only the trustees and directors of invested funds, who administer them at their good pleasure.
This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who. because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying, so to speak, the lifeblood to the entire economic body, and grasping, as it were, in their hands the very soul of production, so that no one dare breathe against their will.
Mr. KNOWLES; The hon. member did not read that part.

Quite right; the hon. member did not read that part. I would1 also ask what party in this house has gone farther than the party to which the hon. member belongs in helping to foster those very conditions that are being spoken of. There is a further quotation in the same encyclical that I should like to read:
. . . for it is rightly contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state, since they carry with them an opportunity of domination too great to be left to private individuals without injury to the community at large.
I contend that if we gave full sway to those interests which are so determined to have decontrol, to have everything thrown back into the hands of those who would use the power of their economic dictatorship, it is those people who would bring about an undesirable form of socialism or communism in this country, rather than the C.C.F. or any other group.
May I give one final quotation from an address entitled, "The Catholic Church and the C.C.F.," delivered on the trans-Canada Catholic broadcast, October 24, 1943, by Reverend C. J. Foran, D.D., St. Anthony's Pro-Cathedral, Edmonton, Alberta, in which he said:
Catholic social teaching will permit the nationalization of industries and facilities which must be nationalized to protect or ensure the common good. Thus far we can certainly go. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation advocates

Emergency Powers

the socialization of banking, transportation, communications, electric power and all other industries and services essential to social planning. Among the industries listed as essential to social planning the C.C.F. manifesto included mining, pulp and paper and the distribution of milk, coal and gasoline.
I wish the hon. member for Trinity to pay special attention to this:
The statement issued by the bishops of Canada after their recent conference in Quebec indicates that the gap between the Catholic position which allows for the nationalization of industries that need to be nationalized to protect the common good and the programme of those who call for the socialization of such industries as mining, pulp and paper and the distribution of milk, coal and gasoline-that gap can be bridged with safety.
Again let me express my hope that never again will a member in this august chamber, be he Jew, Gentile, Protestant or Catholic, find it necessary to defend his being in this party or that party because he belongs to a different religious sect or community.
I would say to the house that in our humble way we realize that we are only human beings. As human beings we have our faults and failings. As a human organization the party to which I have the honour to belong also has its shortcomings. But even so has the House of Commons its shortcomings, simply because it is a human institution. And so long as we bear in mind the ultimate end for which our Creator created us, and the destiny toward which we are all working, I hope that we may humbly walk in that way.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I have but a few observations to make, and I should like to deal with them as they affect the riding I have the honour to represent.
I wish, first, to deal with butter, and the price control of that product. The ultimate result is, of course, a reduction in production. Along with that comes the threat of oleomargarine. It is a threat to the dairy farmers of Canada. May I observe right here that if it is proper to protect industry and to protect labour, it is equally proper to protect the farmer from the importation of this product of cheap labour.
Another indication of the threat to farmers lies in the importation of New Zealand butter. In an order for return tabled some time ago, it was shown that the farmers of New Zealand were receiving 28-35 cents a pound for butter. I would ask the socialists to my left to explain how the farmers in New Zealand can be prosperous when selling butter at that price.
Another factor which enters into the picture lies in the fact that we spent $24 million a

year on butter subsidies. During the war years we were told that we paid only half of our expenditures in this direction, the remainder being borrowed. In other words, $12 million a year that was spent on butter subsidies is still to be paid. Our children's children will be paying for butter, milk and other subsidized foods consumed during the war years. I do not believe they will find it as easy to pay as we would have found it.
People have money to buy luxuries. They buy drinks of all kinds, and yet they want to have their milk subsidized. In this connection, may I make a few comparisons. On February 12, while butter was selling at forty-four cents a pound, Mr. Coulter, a general merchant in my home town, gave me figures showing that the price of lard was twenty-seven cents a pound; shortening, thirty cents, Mazola oil, thirty-seven cents, and Lux soap flakes, thirty-two cents. No one complained about those prices, but they did complain about increases in the price of butter.	It is easy to bear down on the
farmer who did not object to these things being done in the city, where no objection was made to increases in the price of manufactured products. But the little increases paid on farm products-oh, they were terrible!
The milk subsidies alone amount to about one-half the money paid out in family allowances. But people did not want to use family allowances to buy milk; they wanted those moneys for other luxuries, while at the same time subsidizing milk consumption.
At this time I should like to say a word or two about steel and hardware controls. Certainly they are working to a disadvantage, so far as the farmers in Middlesex county are concerned. Ilderton farmers cooperative say that lumber has never been so scarce. Farmers needing lumber for repairs have found it impossible to obtain it. Letters from Thorndale, Hyde Park, Dorchester and Glanworth complain of shortages. Small villages and towns in my community say that farmers are asked to produce in quantity and to maintain quality, while at the same time accepting immigrant labour. And what do they get for it? They get no nails, no lumber, no steel, no wire and no roofing.
A recent fire destroyed a service garage in the town of Lambeth. I was approached to have some steel made available so that quick repairs could be made in order to enable the proprietor to continue to give service to farm tractors, cars and trucks in the community. The steel controller advised me that there was no steel control, and that if I could obtain it from the manufacturer it would be all right. I approached a certain manufacturer and he

Emergency Powers
said, "Yes, you can have the steel." But about the time it was to be delivered someone said, "No, you cannot have it." And, there is no roof on that garage yet.
Recently the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) stated there was no shortage of nails. After he was questioned, it developed that those nails were of aluminum. They were about three times the regular price, and certainly were not suitable for farm repairs since, in many instances, hard lumber is used in farm equipment and construction.
Hyde Park reports that there are no nails in the stores in that area, and none in sight-at the wholesalers. Dorchester reports a very short supply of nails, and not enough spikes in town to build a hog trough. There are no steel troughs. Farm buildings are in need of repair. There are no nails, and there is no lumber or roofing.
From Glanworth one dealer says that he had only one keg of nails in six months, no wire of any kind for a year. Another report indicates that from June, 1946, to January, 1947, there were three kegs of nails, but wire and many sizes of nails were unobtainable. Poultry fencing, hooks and staples were unobtainable. Roofing paper and tar paper were very scarce, while harvesting tools, forks and repairs, as well as other kinds of hardware, were almost unobtainable.
It is true, too, that good, decent farm overalls cannot be obtained. Let me say a word or two about barbed wire. On March 20, I had on the order paper a question to which a reply was given. Among other things I inquired about the kind and tonnage of steel that was used, and how much was saved in changing over from heavy gauge to the lighter war-time gauge. I shall read the paragraph which deals with that particularly:
Based on the 1939 to 1941 average, the consumption of steel for the years 1942 to 1945 inclusive would have amounted to 71.224 net tons. Actually 58,829 net tons were used during this period for the production of barbed wire, therefore, a total of 12,395 net tons were made available for more essential products.
I submit that not only the amount they mention as being saved, but the whole 58.829 tons of steel was wasted. Farmers who bought that wire and put it up a year ago have not a decent, fence today. The whole business was wasted. They might better have made a few rolls of good barbed wire and let the rest go, because, as it is, these farmers have spent the money and they have nothing to show for it. It is about time the manufacturers started to make some decent wire for the farmers.

I wish to say a word or two about rent controls. Rent controls have developed1 a lot of injustices and many crooked practices. I have in mind two houses in my own riding in east London. These houses are not more than two hundred yards apart and are identical in construction and size. One house rents for $23 a month, but the man who owns it cannot get into it. He rents two rooms in an identical house a short distance away, for which he pays $36 a month for the two rooms. These houses are of practically the same value. If there is any justice in that I should like to know about it.
The reason so many people are anxious to retain rent controls is that they have a minority group over a barrel and at a disadvantage. If it were not for that they would not want these controls. The same applies to food controls. The farmers are getting tired of feeding the world and getting the lowest labour return of any class in the country, while having to work longer hours than anyone else. Along with this, they are being denied the goods they need to maintain their farms and homes.
On motion of Mr. White (Middlesex East) the debate was adjourned.
